results.note: MAPP1 Results › Efficacy, 1st paragraph and Fig. 2a legend: n = 89 (46 on MDMA), difference 11.9 (95% CI 6.3-17.4), P < 0.0001, d.f. 71; de facto n = 90, P < 0.0001, d.f. 72. All match.

Efficacy 2nd paragraph: -24.4 (s.d. 11.6, n = 42) vs -13.9 (s.d. 11.5, n = 37); 3rd paragraph: d 0.91 (0.44-1.37, pooled s.d. 11.55) and 0.97 (0.51-1.42). Recomputed the editors' check: the completers' pooled SD is 11.55, 10.5/11.55 = 0.91, while 11.9/11.55 = 1.03.

Efficacy 7th paragraph: 28/42 (67%) vs 12/37 (32%); remission 14/42 (33%) vs 2/37 (5%). Fig. 3 title gives 46 and 44; the bars carry no printed values but their heights match about 61% and 27%. Recomputed: 60.9% vs 27.3%, difference 33.6 points (Wald 95% CI 14.3 to 52.9); remission 30.4% vs 4.5%. Note: 46 and 44 are the arms randomized and dosed (mITT); 91 were randomized and the registry flow shows 45 starting on placebo, so 'all randomized' is the paper's own wording for the mITT.
Efficacy 4th paragraph and Fig. 2b: P = 0.0116, d.f. 71, effect size 0.43 (-0.01 to 0.88), pooled s.d. 2.53; completers -3.1 (2.6) vs -2.0 (2.4).

ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03537014 (API v2): first submitted 2018-05-14, first posted 2018-05-25, start 2018-11-21; primary outcome change in CAPS-5, baseline to 18 weeks post enrollment confirmation; LS mean change -24.5 (-28.28 to -20.71) vs -12.64 (-16.61 to -8.66), denominators 46 and 44, mITT. Registry history: the primary outcome is unchanged since version 0 (24 May 2018); the secondary outcome registered then was BDI-II change plus vital signs, replaced by the SDS on 19 July 2019 (version 26), during enrolment.

Methods › Participants, 1st paragraph (DSM-5 PTSD of 6 months or more, CAPS-5 of 35 or more at baseline after medication washout; the exclusions as stated) and Table 1 totals: CAPS-5 44.1 (6.04), comorbid major depression 82 (91.1%), White 69 (76.7%).

Discussion, 10th paragraph (short-term pre-specified outcome 2 months after the last experimental session; long-term follow-up data to be collected; blinding not formally assessed, challenging, possibly expectation effects) and Methods › Follow-up (data to be published later).

MAPP2 Results › Primary outcomes (single paragraph) and Fig. 2a: -23.7 (-26.94, -20.44) vs -14.8 (-18.28, -11.28); difference -8.9 (-13.70, -4.12), P < 0.001, d 0.7; de facto -23.7 vs -14.8, P < 0.001.

Exploratory outcomes, 1st paragraph: 45/52 (86.5%) vs 29/42 (69.0%); 37/52 (71.2%) vs 20/42 (47.6%); 24/52 (46.2%) vs 9/42 (21.4%); Fig. 3 prints the same after-session-3 values. Recomputed: 37/53 = 69.8%, 20/51 = 39.2%, difference 30.6 points (Wald 12.4 to 48.8).

Fig. 1 (CONSORT): 53 and 51 randomized; on MDMA 1 chose to stop after session 3; on placebo 5 stopped after session 1 and 3 after session 2; 52 and 42 in the de jure analysis. Results › Demographics, 1st paragraph and Discussion, 3rd paragraph give 1.9% (1/53) and 15.7% (8/51).

Methods › Participants (CAPS-5 of 28 or more; tapered off all psychiatric medicines) and Results › Demographics, 2nd paragraph: baseline CAPS-5 39.0 (6.6); 28/104 (26.9%) moderate, 76/104 (73.1%) severe; 35 (33.7%) other than White, 28 (26.9%) Hispanic/Latino.

Discussion, 5th (no evaluation beyond 2 months after therapy), 6th (superiority over SSRIs cannot be assumed without a direct comparison) and 7th paragraphs (the placebo-arm effect could suggest standalone value of the manualized therapy).
Exploratory outcomes, 3rd paragraph: 49/52 (94.2%) and 33/44 (75.0%) certain or thought they had received what they received.

Acknowledgements, 2nd paragraph: funded by MAPS (with support from the Steven and Alexandra Cohen Foundation), organized by MAPS PBC, which oversaw collection, analysis and interpretation. I compared MAPP2's 19 named authors with MAPP1's 38 citation authors: all but Brooke Balliett (thanked as a study therapist in MAPP1) are MAPP1 authors, so 18 of 19 holds.

results.note: The five databases and the May 2025 rerun are in the Methods (p. 2, one paragraph), not in the Results paragraphs named. The trial count, the comparator split (three inactive placebo, three low-dose MDMA, p. 3) and 'all six with MAPS conflicts' (p. 8) are where stated. The search keywords themselves included MAPS and 'breakthrough therapy' (Methods), which matters for any use of 'all six linked to MAPS'.
Exploratory outcomes, 3rd paragraph: every count matches, including the reasons (45/52, 29/52, 28/44). Recomputed Bang index: (49-1)/52 = 0.92 and (33-9)/44 = 0.55.

Methods › Randomization and masking, 2nd paragraph (assessors blinded to general design, visit, assignment, number of treatments and safety data; one CAPS-5 per assessor per participant; participants told to withhold their opinion) and 3rd paragraph (survey at study termination, visit 20). No assessor guesses appear anywhere in the main text.
Discussion, 8th paragraph: expectancy not measured, the three observations as listed. Quotation verbatim (8 words).

Fig. 1: 5 of the 8 placebo discontinuations followed session 1 (3 chose to stop, 1 chose to stop with no outcome data, 1 adverse event). Fig. 3 prints 39.6 vs 22.0 for loss of diagnosis after session 1. Discussion, 3rd paragraph names disappointment from ineffective blinding. For balance: Fig. 2a shows mean CAPS-5 only about 3 points apart after session 1 with overlapping s.e.m. bars, which is what the authors' 'no separation' observation rests on.
MAPP1 Discussion, 10th paragraph: at least 10%; at least 7/44 (15.9%) and 2/46 (4.3%); called anecdotal; site therapists collected safety data, perhaps limiting the blinding of those data.

Methods › Randomization, masking and bias minimization, 2nd paragraph (inactive placebo determined with the FDA; low-dose MDMA improved blinding in phase 2 but was less effective than inactive placebo, citing ref. 15) and 3rd paragraph (observer-blind central rater pool by live video; participants told to withhold their opinion).
MAPP1 Table 1 totals: 29 (32.2) and 19 (21.1).

Brett & Bynum p. 8, Study limitations (single paragraph): blinding maintained or partly maintained in two of six, both with active placebo; functional unblinding in 66.7%. Table 5 (p. 7): 2011 pilot, inactive placebo, 95% of participants correct.
Reply p. 1691, 6th paragraph: blinding a tremendous challenge with no perfect solution (the reply presents it as Burke and Blumberger's point) and no flawless comparator.
MAPP1 Results › Safety, 1st paragraph: the five events, the transient rises in blood pressure and heart rate and 38.1 C in two MDMA participants, as stated.
Registry adverse-events module (threshold 5%; first experimental session to termination visit, about 18 weeks): every listed count matches; serious 0/46 vs 2/44; deaths 0.

Results › Safety, 2nd paragraph and Table 2: SAEs 0 vs 2 (4.5%) (one suicide attempt, one suicidal ideation with self-hospitalization; three events in all); suicidality AESIs 3 (6.5) vs 5 (11.4); cardiac AESIs 0 vs 1 (2.3); the AESI category the paper calls 'abuse potential' 0 vs 0.
Results › Safety, 3rd paragraph: 17/46 (37%) and 14/44 (32%) at baseline; never exceeded baseline; serious ideation almost entirely on placebo (Fig. 4).

Methods › Procedures, 1st paragraph: anticipated effects (euphoria, stimulation, feelings of closeness) intentionally not solicited as adverse events, to avoid biasing collection. Quotation verbatim (5 words). Note for the claims: the source says these effects were not solicited, not that they were not recorded.
Methods › Statistics and reproducibility, 10th paragraph (at least a twofold difference) and Discussion, 10th paragraph (site therapists collected safety data).

Methods › Procedures, 2nd paragraph (AESI terms for addiction, dependence, intentional product misuse, overdose and drug diversion) and Main, 4th paragraph (three doses in a controlled clinical environment with a trained therapy team).
Registry other adverse events: Substance Use [Social circumstances] 3/46 vs 0/44; no euphoria term at the 5% threshold; neither the article's Results nor its Table 2 mentions substance-use events.

MAPP2 Table 2 and Results › Safety, 1st paragraph: 53 (100) vs 49 (96.1); severe 5 (9.4) vs 2 (3.9); serious 0 vs 0; leading to discontinuation 0 vs 2 (3.9); TEAESI 6 (11.3) vs 3 (5.9), none in the TEAESI categories for misuse, physical dependence, diversion or what the paper calls 'abuse'; the four event rows match.

Results › Safety, 2nd paragraph (cardiac 7 vs 1; palpitations 5 (9.4%) vs 1 (2.0%); tachycardia 2 (3.8%) vs 0; vascular 7 vs 2, one moderate hypertension) and 3rd paragraph (transient rises needed no clinical intervention).
Results › Safety, 4th paragraph (44 (83.0%) vs 37 (72.5%); severe 3 vs 2; suicidality TEAESIs 2 vs 2) and 5th paragraph (three participants, five occasions; never exceeded baseline).

Methods › Outcomes, 3rd paragraph (window, site-physician severity, relatedness not assessed except for serious events, the >10% and twofold rule) and Statistical analysis, 4th paragraph (twofold difference).

Discussion, 4th paragraph (substance use disorder exclusions; current serious imminent suicide risk excluded; long-term data needed on misuse) and 6th paragraph (high suicide risk, personality disorders, cardiovascular disease).
Brett & Bynum p. 4, Safety 1st paragraph (reporting varied substantially, partly by measure) and p. 9, the 1st paragraph starting on that page (inconsistent documentation made synthesis challenging).

corrected.extracted: MAPP1 reported few serious adverse effects, but trials of phase 3 size without long-term follow-up cannot assess rare events reliably, and such events can emerge once a treatment is in wide use.

results.note: Place and role are right (p. 1689, 5th paragraph), but the letter does not say 'only': it says rare events can become noticeable when a treatment is widely implemented. Dropping 'only' and adding the letter's own premise gives the corrected text.

MAPP2 Results › Primary outcomes: -8.9 (-13.70, -4.12), P < 0.001; placebo LS mean change -14.8.
MAPP2 Exploratory outcomes, 3rd paragraph (94.2% and 75.0%) and Discussion, 8th paragraph (expectancy not measured).
MAPP1 Discussion, 10th paragraph.
MAPP2 Discussion, 5th paragraph: evaluations did not extend beyond 2 months after therapy; ongoing follow-up NCT05066282.
MAPP1 Methods › Procedures, 1st paragraph (not solicited) and Discussion, 10th paragraph (site therapists).

Methods › Randomization, 2nd paragraph cites ref. 15; reference 15 is Mithoefer et al. (2019), the pooled analysis of six phase 2 trials (Psychopharmacology 236, 2735-2745). The power calculation also used pooled phase 2 data (Statistics and reproducibility, 1st paragraph).

Brett & Bynum p. 2, Study and participant characteristics, 1st paragraph: two tabled articles retracted in August 2024, both including data from a site where a serious ethical violation occurred (DOIs given); the review links the violation to the retractions explicitly on p. 9. The review misnames the journal (Journal of Psychopharmacology), which the anchor rightly does not repeat.
Brett & Bynum p. 9, right column, the 2nd paragraph starting on that page: no citation in the paragraph; vote, conclusions and concerns as listed.
Brett & Bynum p. 4, Efficacy 1st paragraph and Table 2: 5 of 6 significant; Oehen et al. (2013) against a 25 mg active placebo, not significant (p = 0.0666, Appendix p. 12).

corrected.extracted: The critics argue that a breakthrough label requires benchmarking against first-line trauma-focused psychotherapies, which on cross-trial figures reach similar or greater symptom reductions (SMDs 0.83 to 2.07 against control, wait-list or usual care, against MAPP1's 0.91 against placebo with the same therapy) with half or less of the therapy time MAPP1 required (the equivalent of 28 sessions of 90 minutes, with two therapists in every session).

results.note: The letter says the first-line psychotherapies attain 'similar or elevated' symptom reduction (3rd paragraph), not only similar; the cited SMDs run from 0.83 to 2.07 against control, wait-list or usual care. The therapy-time comparison (6th paragraph, continued on p. 1690) and the call for benchmarking (1st paragraph of each page) are at the places given.
Reply p. 1691, 4th to 6th paragraphs, as stated.
